<problem>
All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. A graph is $H$-free if it contains no subgraph, not necessarily induced, isomorphic to $H$. Write $e(G)$ for the number of edges of $G$, and $c(G)$ for its number of simple cycles of length at least three, counted without orientation or a chosen starting vertex. For a fixed graph $H$, define
\[
\operatorname{ex}(n,H)=\max\{e(G):|V(G)|=n,\ G\text{ is }H\text{-free}\},
\qquad
\operatorname{cyc}(n,H)=\max\{c(G):|V(G)|=n,\ G\text{ is }H\text{-free}\}.
\]
Let $\chi(H)$ denote the minimum number of colors in a proper vertex coloring of $H$. Let $T_{n,r}$ be the complete $r$-partite graph on $n$ vertices whose part sizes differ by at most one, allowing empty parts, and put $t_r(n)=e(T_{n,r})$.

For each integer $r\ge2$, let $\mathcal S_r$ be the set of real numbers $a\ge0$ for which there exist a fixed graph $H$ with $\chi(H)=r+1$, a constant $C\ge0$, and a positive integer $N_0$ satisfying both conditions:

1. For every integer $N\ge N_0$,
\[
\operatorname{ex}(N,H)\le t_r(N)+aN+C.
\]
2. For infinitely many positive integers $n$, there is no $n$-vertex $H$-free graph $G$ satisfying simultaneously
\[
e(G)=\operatorname{ex}(n,H)
\quad\text{and}\quad
c(G)=\operatorname{cyc}(n,H).
\]

The choices of $H,C,N_0$ may depend on $r$ and $a$, but not on $N$ or $n$. Determine $\mathcal S_r$ explicitly for every integer $r\ge2$, including whether its finite boundary points belong to it.
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer must give an explicit description of the set \(\mathcal S_r\subseteq[0,\infty)\) for every integer \(r\ge2\), specifying exactly which real numbers belong to it and whether each finite boundary point is included.

A team of 4 agents was told that the answer is \mathcal S_2=[\tfrac12,\infty),\qquad \mathcal S_r=(\tfrac1r,\infty)\ \text{for every }r\ge3. and asked to prove it (told: Proving it takes two halves: for \(r=2\) and every \(a\ge\frac12\), and for every \(r\ge3\) and every \(a>\frac1r\), there exist a fixed graph \(H\) with \(\chi(H)=r+1\), a constant \(C\ge0\), and a positive integer \(N_0\) such that \(\operatorname{ex}(N,H)\le t_r(N)+aN+C\) for every \(N\ge N_0\), yet for infinitely many \(n\) no \(n\)-vertex \(H\)-free graph simultaneously attains \(\operatorname{ex}(n,H)\) edges and \(\operatorname{cyc}(n,H)\) cycles; whereas for \(r=2\) and every \(0\le a<\frac12\), and for every \(r\ge3\) and every \(0\le a\le\frac1r\), every fixed graph \(H\) with \(\chi(H)=r+1\) satisfying \(\operatorname{ex}(N,H)\le t_r(N)+aN+C\) for some constant \(C\ge0\) and all sufficiently large \(N\) has, for every sufficiently large \(n\), an \(n\)-vertex \(H\)-free graph simultaneously attaining \(\operatorname{ex}(n,H)\) edges and \(\operatorname{cyc}(n,H)\) cycles.), writing Python that checks every step. Their run ended: all agents idle, the judge found the proof complete. The answer they were told may be wrong: teams told a wrong answer sometimes stop at bounds or partial results, and sometimes claim a proof anyway. You decide whether this team proved \mathcal S_2=[\tfrac12,\infty),\qquad \mathcal S_r=(\tfrac1r,\infty)\ \text{for every }r\ge3.: whether a search for the answer can stop here and report \mathcal S_2=[\tfrac12,\infty),\qquad \mathcal S_r=(\tfrac1r,\infty)\ \text{for every }r\ge3. as proved.

- unfinished: they don't claim a complete proof of \mathcal S_2=[\tfrac12,\infty),\qquad \mathcal S_r=(\tfrac1r,\infty)\ \text{for every }r\ge3..
